title: Christabel, Part I: composition and publication
short: Part I was written at Nether Stowey in 1797, Part II at Keswick in 1800; the unfinished poem was published only in 1816.
body: Coleridge's 1816 Preface dates the first part to 1797 and the second to 1800. It was meant for the second edition of Lyrical Ballads (1800), but in October 1800 Wordsworth decided against printing it, a blow that deepened Coleridge's doubts about his powers. The poem circulated in manuscript and recitation for sixteen years: Walter Scott heard it recited and borrowed its metre for The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805), and Byron, who admired it, urged John Murray to publish it. It appeared in 1816 with 'Kubla Khan' and 'The Pains of Sleep'. Coleridge never wrote the promised further parts. These notes cover Part I and its Conclusion.

title: The 'new principle' of metre
short: Coleridge claimed the metre counts four accents a line while syllables vary from seven to twelve; the first line already has eleven syllables.
body: In the 1816 Preface Coleridge says the metre is founded on 'counting in each line the accents, not the syllables', with four accents but anywhere from seven to twelve syllables, the variation matching shifts in 'imagery or passion'. The opening line, with its rocking anapaests, shows the licence at once, and the third line, 'Tu--whit!--Tu--whoo!', breaks the pattern into sound effect. Later prosodists argued that most of the poem is ordinary four-stress iambic verse with substitutions, and that the principle was hardly new, since it occurs in old ballads and in Middle English. The metre's flexibility nonetheless allowed the poem's sudden hesitations, questions and repetitions.

title: Sir Leoline
short: Christabel's widowed father; the name, from leo (lion), suits a proud baron of Border romance, and his household lives under his wife's death.
body: The setting is a Border castle in the north of England (Part II names Langdale and Tryermaine in Cumbria). Leoline's name may suggest 'lion', in keeping with his rank and temper. His wife died giving birth to Christabel, and the household is shaped by that loss: the mastiff seems to see 'my lady's shroud', the castle bell recalls her, and in Part II every matin bell 'knells us back to a world of death'. The ballad-like phrase 'the Baron rich' sets the tone of a minstrel tale. Nethercot traced the name and setting to Coleridge's reading in Border antiquities and romance.

title: The toothless mastiff
short: The old bitch howls sixteen times at midnight, once for each quarter-chime and stroke; she is the castle's half-comic, half-uncanny sense of the supernatural.
body: At midnight the clock strikes four quarters and twelve hours, and the mastiff answers with 'Sixteen short howls'. 'Some say, she sees my lady's shroud': animals in folklore were believed to sense ghosts. The grotesque, deliberately homely detail made some early reviewers laugh, but it prepares a key moment: when Geraldine enters, the sleeping dog makes 'an angry moan' (l. 148), as it never has before. The narrator's 'Some say' introduces the poem's habit of rumour and hesitant report.

anchor: Is the night chilly and dark?
title: Question and answer
short: The narrator asks questions and answers them, a ballad device that builds suspense and makes the reader share his uncertainty.
body: 'Is the night chilly and dark? / The night is chilly, but not dark.' The narrator's voice, like a minstrel's, asks and corrects itself; later it hesitates ('I guess', 'belike', 'What sees she there?'). Critics have linked this to the poem's central uncertainty about what Christabel sees and what Geraldine is: the teller seems to know less than the tale. Coleridge's 1816 Preface promised further parts, and later reports of his plans for the ending (for instance Gillman's) do not agree with one another. The device of question and answer imitates old ballads such as 'Edward'.

title: A month before May
short: It is April: spring is late in coming, and the 'one red leaf' of last year still hangs on the oak.
body: The time is April, early spring delayed ('the Spring comes slowly up this way'). The bare forest, chill air and full but dim moon create a threshold season, neither winter nor spring, suited to a poem about transition and ambiguity. Coleridge was writing at Nether Stowey, and some readers find observed detail of the Quantock woods behind the poem's landscape.

title: Oak and mistletoe
short: Mistletoe is rare on oak; to the Druids such mistletoe was sacred, so the setting has a pre-Christian, magical aura.
body: Mistletoe grows chiefly on apple and other trees, and rarely on oak. Pliny the Elder (Natural History 16.249-251) describes the Druids cutting it from the oak as a sacred plant. Christabel goes to the 'huge oak tree' to pray for her absent knight, a Christian act in a pagan place, and finds Geraldine on the other side of that same tree. The spelling 'misletoe' is the archive's.

title: The one red leaf
short: A single surviving leaf dances on the topmost twig in windless air: a precise natural image that is also eerie, because nothing seems to move it.
body: Dorothy Wordsworth's Alfoxden journal for 7 March 1798 records the one remaining leaf on a tree dancing in the wind, and critics have long compared it with these lines; which way any borrowing ran between the two households is uncertain. There is 'not wind enough' to move a curl or the leaf, yet the leaf 'dances as often as dance it can': something stirs that is not the wind. The image of the 'last of its clan' can also be read as a figure of Christabel, alone and motherless.

title: Jesu, Maria, shield her well!
short: The narrator's prayer, a refrain that recurs at the end of Part II, frames Christabel as a Catholic innocent under spiritual threat.
body: The invocation of Jesus and Mary in Latinate forms sets the poem in a medieval Catholic world. Christabel herself cries 'Mary mother, save me now!' on seeing Geraldine, and Geraldine's reaction to the Virgin's name is a sign of what she is. The refrain returns at the very moment, in Part II, when Geraldine's eyes shrink to a serpent's. The narrator's prayers are part of the poem's pattern of protective utterance that cannot, in the end, protect.

title: Geraldine: what is she?
short: The beautiful stranger in white, with bare 'blue-veined feet' and gems in her hair, may be a witch, lamia, vampire or fallen spirit; the poem never says.
body: Geraldine shows many signs of supernatural evil from folklore: she must be carried over the threshold, she cannot praise the Virgin, the dog moans and the fire flares as she passes, and her bosom bears a terrible 'mark'. Readers have taken her as a witch or vampire; Coleridge's friend James Gillman reported that the continuation was to turn on the return of Christabel's absent lover, by whom Geraldine would be defeated. Twentieth-century critics added psychological and sexual readings, in which Geraldine is Christabel's own repressed desire, or a seductress in a story of same-sex attraction. Karen Swann reads the poem as deliberately unresolved. The name may recall Surrey's 'Fair Geraldine' sonnet.

title: Geraldine's story
short: Geraldine claims abduction by five warriors on white palfreys: a story of romance clichés whose vagueness ('I have no thought what men they be') invites suspicion.
body: A 'palfrey' is a gentle riding horse for a lady. The tale of abduction belongs to chivalric romance and allows Christabel to play the rescuing host. Its details are vague and unverifiable, and Geraldine even says she has 'lain entranced' (in a trance). In Part II she will name her father, Lord Roland de Vaux of Tryermaine, Leoline's estranged friend, a claim that wins her the baron's protection. 'Yestermorn' is an archaic compound (yesterday morning).

title: I wis
short: 'I wis' is a false archaism meaning 'I know' or 'certainly', formed by misreading the old adverb 'ywis' (certainly) as 'I wis'.
body: Middle English 'ywis' or 'iwis' was an adverb meaning 'certainly' (Old English gewis). Later writers misread it as a pronoun and verb, 'I wis', taken as 'I know'. Coleridge uses it twice (also in the Conclusion, 'yet, I wis'). Such archaisms ('belike', 'countree', 'wel-a-day') give the poem the flavour of old romance and of Percy's Reliques, a mode Coleridge and Wordsworth both drew on in 1797-98.

anchor: Over the threshold of the gate
title: Carried over the threshold
short: Geraldine sinks at the gate and must be lifted across: in folklore, evil spirits cannot enter a house unless invited and carried in.
body: At the gate 'ironed within and without' Geraldine collapses 'belike through pain', and Christabel lifts her 'a weary weight' over the threshold, after which 'the lady rose again, / And moved, as she were not in pain'. Folklore held that witches and demons could not cross a blessed or protected threshold of their own will; Christabel's charity is the invitation. The gesture also parodies a bridal custom, since Christabel carries Geraldine in as a husband carries a bride, which supports readings of the poem's sexual ambiguity.

anchor: Praise we the Virgin all divine
title: Geraldine cannot praise the Virgin
short: When Christabel invites her to thank the Virgin, Geraldine pleads weariness: a hint, by folklore logic, that she cannot utter holy names.
body: 'Alas! alas! said Geraldine, / I cannot speak for weariness.' The excuse repeats her earlier words, and the narrator doubles the couplet 'So free from danger, free from fear', a repetition that sounds increasingly ironic. Readers alert to signs of the demonic notice the evasion; the poem itself only reports it. This is one of a sequence of small warnings (threshold, dog, flame) that Christabel, in her innocence, does not read.

title: The mastiff's moan
short: The sleeping dog, which has never howled at Christabel, moans in her sleep as Geraldine passes: animals sense the uncanny.
body: The narrator tries to explain it away ('Perhaps it is the owlet's scritch', a dialect form of 'screech'), but the repetition of 'what can ail the mastiff bitch?' underlines the warning. The word 'bitch' troubled some readers in 1816, but it is used in its plain sense of a female dog. The dog's sleeping response belongs to the poem's world of half-conscious perception, where things are sensed but not understood.

title: The flaring brands
short: The dying fire leaps up as Geraldine passes, showing Christabel only 'the lady's eye' and the boss of her father's shield.
body: 'Brands' are burning logs. The sudden flame is another supernatural sign, and what it shows is suggestive: Geraldine's eye, an emblem of the gaze that in Part II will shrink to a serpent's, and the 'boss' (central knob) of Sir Leoline's shield, emblem of the father's protective power, hanging useless in a 'murky old niche'. 'O softly tread' reminds us that the father sleeps and cannot help.

title: The lamp at the angel's feet
short: Christabel's chamber is carved with strange figures 'out of the carver's brain', and her silver lamp hangs from an angel's feet.
body: The chamber, 'carved so curiously', is a space of art and imagination; the lamp on its 'twofold silver chain' fastened to a carved angel suggests a protective, sacred presence. Christabel 'trims' it (cuts the wick so it burns bright), and leaves it 'swinging to and fro' as Geraldine sinks to the floor. Some critics see in the room a picture of the mind itself, its imagery 'made out of the carver's brain'.

title: The wine and the mother's spirit
short: Christabel offers wine her dead mother made; Geraldine wishes the mother present, then drives away her guardian spirit: 'Off, wandering mother!'
body: A 'cordial' is a restorative drink (from Latin cor, heart), and this 'wine of virtuous powers', distilled from wild flowers, links Christabel to her dead mother. Christabel tells of the prophecy that the mother would hear the castle bell 'Strike twelve upon my wedding-day'. Geraldine's 'I would ... she were!' changes at once into a struggle with an invisible presence: 'Off, wandering mother! ... this hour is mine'. The scene implies that the mother's ghost is Christabel's guardian, and that Geraldine has power to banish it. Swann reads the 'wandering mother' as central to the poem's anxieties about female power and literary form.

title: Peak and pine
short: An echo of the witches' curse in Macbeth, 'Shall he dwindle, peak and pine': to 'peak' is to waste away.
body: In Macbeth 1.3 the First Witch curses a sailor: 'Weary se'nnights nine times nine / Shall he dwindle, peak and pine'. To 'peak' meant to grow thin and sickly. Geraldine's use of the witches' words is one of the clearest textual signs that Coleridge was drawing on the language of witchcraft. 'I have power to bid thee flee' asserts a spiritual authority that the poem does not explain.

title: Geraldine's bosom
short: As Geraldine undresses, Christabel sees her bosom and side: the printed text withholds what she sees, which a manuscript line made explicit.
body: The dash after 'half her side' marks a deliberate gap. Hazlitt's hostile review in The Examiner (2 June 1816) complained that Coleridge had omitted a line needed to understand the story, quoting it (inexactly) as 'Hideous, deformed, and pale of hue'. Part II confirms that the bosom is 'old' and 'cold'. By omitting the line, Coleridge made the moment an enigma: the narrator's 'not to tell' doubles Geraldine's spell, which will forbid Christabel to speak. Critics read the mark as a witch's mark, a sign of age and corruption, or the 'seal' of Geraldine's own suffering ('This mark of my shame, this seal of my sorrow').

anchor: In the touch of this bosom
title: The spell of silence
short: Geraldine's spell makes her 'lord of thy utterance': Christabel will know the truth but be unable to tell it, the poem's central theme of silenced speech.
body: The metre changes here into longer, anapaestic lines, marking the spell. Geraldine allows Christabel only one permitted story, the innocent one: that she heard a moaning in the forest and brought home a lady 'in love and in charity'. In Part II Christabel can say only 'All will yet be well' and cannot explain her terror to her father. The theme of knowledge without speech links the poem with Coleridge's lifelong concern with will, guilt and the blocked utterance.

title: "For his is alone in": a textual problem
short: The archive's 'his' is almost certainly a misreading of 'this' (as in 1816 and later texts): 'this is alone in thy power to declare'.
body: Standard editions read 'For this is alone in / Thy power to declare', that is, the only thing you will be able to say is the following innocent account. The text printed here has 'his', which makes no grammatical sense and seems to be a printing error. The irregular short lines of this passage were themselves unusual in 1816. Students should read the sense as 'this alone is in your power to declare'.

anchor: As a mother with her child
title: Conclusion to Part I: mother and child
short: The Conclusion returns to Christabel praying at the oak and then shows Geraldine holding her 'As a mother with her child': care and possession in one image.
body: The Conclusion, in quieter verse, contrasts Christabel's prayer at the old oak with her sleep in Geraldine's arms, 'With open eyes ... Asleep, and dreaming fearfully'. The simile of mother and child is the poem's most disturbing, because Geraldine has just banished Christabel's actual mother. The 'worker of these harms' seems to 'slumber still and mild'. Critics have read the image both as predatory possession and as a hint that Geraldine is herself a victim seeking comfort, an ambiguity that Coleridge's reported plans for the ending never resolved.

title: tairn; fell
short: A 'tairn' (tarn) is a small mountain lake and a 'fell' a hill: northern dialect words that place the poem in the Lake District.
body: 'Tarn' comes from Old Norse tjorn and is a characteristic Cumbrian word, as is 'fell' (Old Norse fjall, mountain). The northern vocabulary looks ahead to the Lake District geography of Part II, written after Coleridge moved to Keswick in 1800. The hour of Geraldine's power ('one hour was thine') silences the night-birds, whose return, 'tu-whoo! tu-whoo!', echoes the poem's opening and marks the spell's passing.

anchor: the blue sky bends over all
title: "For the blue sky bends over all!"
short: Part I ends with a line of simple faith: saints will help those who call, and heaven covers everyone, Christabel included.
body: The narrator imagines that Christabel's tears and smiles may come from a vision of her guardian spirit or her mother, and ends with an assertion of providence. Some readers take the line as sincere consolation; others hear it as too easy, given what has just happened, and as part of the narrator's well-meaning naivety. The phrase 'youthful hermitess, / Beauteous in a wilderness, / Who, praying always, prays in sleep' presents Christabel's innocence as a kind of unbroken prayer that persists even under the spell.
